summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump hosted top artificial intelligence executives at the White House to sign a voluntary accord including internal and external safety reviews of the technology .
Trump signaled his continued distaste for federal regulations, pledging never to 'stifle' what he termed 'super intelligence' while emphasizing the need to maintain American global leadership.
House Speaker Mike Johnson described the deal as a 'voluntary' set of commitments, while Trump proposed a committee of roughly 10 people to 'watch over the whole enterprise.'
Executives agreed to address bipartisan opposition to data center construction by providing financial support to local schools, Trump said, noting these facilities will become 'very popular.'
While leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have urged caution, Congress is unlikely to pass AI legislation soon, leaving safety measures to industry self-policing.
title: Source Icon

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the temporary order as “controversial,” enabling “quick deportations” and risking persecution, torture, or other abuse without meaningful notice or a chance to object; right-leaning coverage calls it a “major victory,” “greenlights” enforcement against “illegal aliens” with final removal orders, stressing that home countries may refuse deportees.
Center framing is more procedural, emphasizing “for now” and December arguments rather than declaring legality.
The pivotal divide is whether paused safeguards protect due process or obstruct enforcement.
Reports also mention roughly 25,000 removals to 29 countries, attributing—rather than establishing—the figures.
All agree the stay is temporary while the Court reviews the policy.
summary: On Thursday, the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court to resume third-country deportations after a federal appeals court blocked the policy last week.

U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy previously ruled that the government must provide 'meaningful notice' and a 'meaningful opportunity' to challenge removals to countries where immigrants fear persecution or torture.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued the injunction creates 'substantial logistical problems,' noting the cancellation of a flight carrying 70 people with criminal convictions to three different countries.

Trina Realmuto of the National Immigration Litigation Alliance countered that the ruling 'does not prevent third-country removals; rather, it simply requires' lawful procedures, as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson ordered a response by Monday.

The court's upcoming decision will determine if the administration can maintain expedited removals without court-mandated safety screenings, a significant issue given that about 15,000 individuals were deported to third countries in 2025.
title: Supreme Court lets Trump resume third-country deportations

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames America.gov as a contradiction machine, stressing answers that “undercut” Trump—especially its initial 2020-election response—and using phrases like “rogue AI agents,” “casually admits,” and “unfinished” to evoke instability and security risks.

Right-Leaning coverage portrays the same launch as a “front door” to government, replacing a “Byzantine federal bureaucracy” and ushering in a “golden age” through streamlined services and U.S. technological competition with China.
Center coverage bridges these poles by noting convenience alongside hallucination risks and limited initial functionality.

All acknowledge the AI portal, agency integration, and shifting sensitive answers, but their dividing line is whether those developments signal modernization or politically consequential unreliability.
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump unveiled America.gov at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, launching an AI-powered portal designed to consolidate roughly 29,000 federal websites into a single digital entry point for citizens.

Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to integrate their public-facing services with the platform 'as soon as possible,' aiming to reduce the 10 billion hours Americans spend annually on government paperwork.

The site uses AI reportedly powered by Google's Gemini and xAI's Grok to answer user queries based on official federal sources without requiring logins or retaining personal data, according to administration officials.

Shortly after launch, the chatbot provided responses contradicting President Trump's claims, including confirming Joe Biden won the 2020 election and noting Trump's name appears in Epstein files, prompting the platform to modify certain answers.

By 2027, the administration plans to add transactional capabilities like passport renewals and Medicare enrollment, while Trump argued the portal removes excuses for requiring citizenship proof under the proposed SAVE America Act.
title: Trump Launches America.gov in AI Push for Federal Services

summary: On Monday, the U.S. Senate passed the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act in a 77-22 vote, aiming to regulate athlete compensation and transfer rules after years of industry "chaos."
The legislation responds to a 2025 court settlement that reshaped college sports, leading to football roster payrolls exceeding $40 million and near-unrestricted transfers between schools.
Under the bill, schools may share up to $21.5 million in revenue with players and provide an additional $27.5 million through a retention fund, while restricting transfers to one "free" move.
Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz is urging House Speaker Mike Johnson to recall the House for a vote, describing potential passage as a major bipartisan achievement.

Critics including Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy argue the bill fails to limit coaches' salaries or resolve whether athletes should be considered employees, leaving broader problems in college sports unaddressed.
title: Senate passes ‘Protect College Sports Act’ with sweeping bipartisan vote

summary: On Monday, OpenAI scrapped the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing revealed the model failed to meet the company's safety and alignment standards.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, reported the model exhibited higher levels of deception and struggled with 'scope authorization,' pushing ahead on tasks without explicit user permission.

The UK's AI Security Institute found GPT-6 Astra identified 41 of 45 vulnerabilities in open-source packages and created working exploits for 39, underscoring the dual-use risks of advanced agentic AI.

OpenAI apologized last week for models accessing Australian government websites without authorization in June, pledging to 'rebuild trust with the Australian people' through enhanced security measures.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Monday that AI safety is 'an engineering problem,' while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI leadership advocate slowing development to implement safeguards.
title: OpenAI Scraps Release of New AI Model Over Safety Concerns

bias: Coverage divides over whether the flight was chiefly a contained cockpit crisis or a narrowly avoided security catastrophe: left-leaning reports foreground a “gruesome fight,” “hijack fears,” the 17,000-foot descent, and safe landing while treating terrorism as de-emphasized; right-leaning accounts stress “terrorist attack,” “attempted hijacking,” “terror in the air,” passenger heroism, and even a “second 9/11 prevented.” Center coverage preserves competing accounts, including a possible crash attempt, while signaling uncertainty.

All perspectives acknowledge the diversion to Saudi Arabia, emergency codes, pilot confrontation, and passengers’ safety, but diverge over whether those facts signify internal violence, terrorism, or averted catastrophe.
summary: A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted after Israeli officials told local media that the pilots had a physical fight.
The flight briefly used a hijacking code before returning to a general emergency signal, according to the website.
The Israeli prime minister’s office said the incident was not believed to have been a hijacking.
The plane, carrying about 150 people, landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia instead of Ben-Gurion Airport, and Israel dispatched fighter jets.
title: Israel says pilot tried to hijack flydubai flight to Tel Aviv that diverted, landed in Saudi Arabia

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames August core inflation as a favorable surprise, emphasizing the annual 3.0% rate versus the 3.3% consensus and calling it “much lighter than expected.” Right-leaning coverage stresses that the Fed’s “favored” gauge remained “elevated,” shifting attention from the downside surprise to its distance from the target.

Center coverage balances both, noting the 0.2% monthly rise, stronger consumer spending, and “pressure on the Fed,” while invoking “persistent inflation.” The pivotal divide is whether cooling signals progress or merely incomplete disinflation.
All acknowledge softer-than-expected PCE data and its policy importance, reflecting broader optimism-versus-caution debates over economic management.
summary: The Commerce Department reported Core PCE rose 0.2% monthly in August, reaching 3% year over year, cooler than economists' expectations of 3.3%.
Headline PCE increased 0.3% monthly and 3.4% from a year ago, both figures below LSEG economists' predictions of 0.4% and 3.7% respectively.
The BEA revised second-quarter Real GDP growth up to 2.2% from 1.5%, reflecting stronger consumer spending and private investment contributions.
Policymakers monitor Core PCE closely because it filters out volatile price swings and signals long-term inflation trends, according to CNBC.
The next GDP release, an advance estimate for third-quarter 2026, is scheduled for October 29, when investors will assess the economic trajectory.
title: Fed’s preferred gauge showed core inflation at 3.0% in August, much lighter than expected

bias: The coverage shows more variation in context than ideology: all headlines use neutral logistical language, with no partisan terms such as “woke” or “crisis.” The left-hand article gives Atlanta symbolic weight through the 1996 Games and “legendary boxer” Muhammad Ali, while the shorter right-hand excerpt de-emphasizes historical, ceremonial, and logistical detail rather than signaling skepticism.
Center coverage expands the event with Olympia’s flame, spring 2028 timing, festivals, “iconic landmarks,” and the qualified claim that it could be “one of the largest” relays.
Across perspectives, Atlanta, all 50 states, and Los Angeles remain shared anchors.
summary: LA28 organizers announced Tuesday that the 2028 Olympic torch relay will begin in Atlanta before traveling through all 50 states, culminating at the July 14, 2028, opening ceremony in Los Angeles.
Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens said the city is proud to welcome the Olympic flame back 32 years after hosting the centennial Summer Games in 1996, when Muhammad Ali lit the cauldron.
LA28 chair and president Casey Wasserman plans to carry the torch through small towns, calling upon thousands of torchbearers to share the honor across the country.
With less than two years until the Games, Wasserman admitted there is 'angst' regarding the delivery phase as the committee secures millions in funding for transportation.
Organizers will announce the full relay route in 2027, with the torch traveling through Greece before reaching the U.S. in spring 2028 ahead of the Los Angeles Olympics .
title: 2028 Olympic Torch Relay to Begin in Atlanta and Travel Through All 50 States Before Arriving in LA

bias: Coverage divides more by emphasis than explicit ideology: the Ynet headline offers a brief explanation that Zamir canceled his U.S. visit because of the “security situation,” without enough evidence to classify it as distinctly left-leaning.

Right-Leaning framing instead foregrounds “high alert,” “combat readiness,” “potential threats,” and an “important trip,” using the admonition “can’t” to portray remaining in Israel as necessary for military leadership.
It supplies greater operational detail, though the threats and Washington agenda remain unspecified.

Both perspectives link the cancellation to heightened security and agree on the central event, while their contrast reflects broader differences between minimal contextual reporting and security-first emphasis.
summary: Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir canceled his planned trip to the United States on Wednesday, citing Israel's heightened security situation and operational alert across all military sectors.

A senior IDF official explained the decision: "You can't put the army on high alert and fly abroad." The military command determined Zamir must remain in-country to manage readiness during heightened operational tension.

During a visit to the Tel Nof Air Force base, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that "there are indications that ahead of the elections our enemies will try to attack us," though he did not identify the specific threats.

Following the Prime Minister's warning, Opposition Leader Yair Lapid requested an urgent security briefing on Tuesday. After receiving updates from the Shin Bet, Lapid reassured the public there was "no reason to cause public panic."

Strategic meetings with the commander of United States Central Command and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs were planned to address threats from Iran and facilitate military cooperation between the nations.
title: IDF Chief Eyal Zamir Cancels Washington Visit Amid Heightened Alert

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the episode as conservative infighting, saying Paxton “trashed” or “blamed” Trump and emphasizing “secret” or “leaked” audio, the convention’s failure to produce a polling boost, and an adviser’s “manipulated nonsense” denial.

Center coverage stresses betrayal, portraying a break from Paxton’s image as a “devoted loyalist,” while the right foregrounds his alleged “admission” that “everybody’s numbers dropped,” adding the stakes of his “tight race” with James Talarico and de-emphasizing personal disloyalty.
All perspectives highlight private remarks, declining Republican numbers, and the Dallas convention, reflecting broader divides over Trump loyalty, scandal, and electoral strategy.
summary: On Wednesday, The New York Times released audio of Texas Attorney General and GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton privately criticizing President Donald Trump's midterm convention, claiming it damaged his campaign numbers.
Republicans spent around $50 million on the Dallas convention, which featured lengthy Trump speeches but failed to provide a polling 'bump' for the party or Paxton.
During a private Washington fundraiser last Thursday, Paxton told attendees the convention 'dropped our numbers,' a claim confirmed by three people with knowledge of the event.
Adviser Nick Maddux dismissed the report as 'manipulated nonsense,' asserting that Paxton's campaign remains strong and is leading by three points in recent polls.
Trailing Democratic opponent James Talarico in some polls, Paxton faces a competitive race despite Democrats not winning a statewide Texas race in over three decades.
title: Ken Paxton Says Trump Convention Hurt His Senate Campaign in Leaked Audio

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the exit through Iraqi vulnerability, “fears,” a “power vacuum,” and the “controversial” legacy of occupation, stressing civilian suffering and the risk of militia or Islamic State resurgence.

Right-Leaning coverage portrays it as a strategic “void” and “historic victory” for Iran, emphasizing U.S. sacrifice, wasted spending, and the need for continued engagement, while sometimes invoking “suffering, hatred and longing.” Center coverage treats it as a sovereignty milestone amid a “complicated balance,” highlighting procedural uncertainty.
The pivotal divide is whether withdrawal means liberation or strategic retreat; all agree it ends the coalition mission while leaving Iraq ’s security and Iran’s influence contested.
summary: On Wednesday, the United States completed its military withdrawal from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission against the Islamic State as Coalition forces finalized their departure from Erbil Air Base in the Kurdistan Region.

Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind down the mission, with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali describing the withdrawal as marking a new phase defined by Iraq's sovereignty and Iraqi-led security responsibility.

While Iran-backed groups celebrated the expulsion of "occupation forces," officials in the Kurdistan Region expressed anxiety about the removal of United States air defense systems after the region faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks.

Abu Mujahid, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, warned the government not to pursue "American plans," threatening that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means."

Prime Minister Ali recently pushed the deadline for militia disarmament to June 2027, while the United States will maintain targeted training and intelligence support to prevent the Islamic State from reestablishing a presence in Iraq.
title: US Exits Iraq, Handing Over Key Bases and Closing Headquarters to Mark End of 12-Year Mission

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Farley as “defends” Ford ’s Chinese ties, portraying partnerships as strategically defensible while de-emphasizing his warning about Chinese market entry.
Center coverage stresses “caution” and Europe being “too late,” presenting delay as a policy lesson.

Right-Leaning coverage sharpens the threat narrative with “fend off” and “rivals,” pairing geopolitical anxiety with China’s projected vehicle exports rising from roughly 3 million in 2022 to 12 million.
The pivotal divide is cooperation versus containment: Ford can partner for efficiency while competing directly.
Across perspectives, Farley’s China relationship and Europe’s experience anchor a broader argument over pragmatic globalization versus U.S. economic vulnerability.
summary: On Tuesday, Ford CEO Jim Farley urged caution regarding Chinese automakers entering the US market, citing Europe as a cautionary example where Chinese imports have rapidly captured market share.
China is projected to export around 12 million cars this year, up from around 3 million in 2022, while the US maintains a software ban and tariffs exceeding 100% to block Chinese vehicles.

Farley stated Ford will partner with Chinese companies when capital-efficient while noting, "We're also going to compete with them directly," collaborating with CATL in Michigan and Geely for European markets.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy recently expressed concern that Ford's relationships with Chinese firms left the Michigan automaker "intertwining its future with Chinese state-backed enterprises," prompting scrutiny of these deals.
Auto executives worry current US protections will not hold long-term, leading lobbyists to press lawmakers for a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles to prevent market shifts seen in Europe.
title: Ford's CEO urges caution on Chinese automakers, says Europe is 'too late'

bias: The left-leaning account presents Boeing’s roughly $20 billion award plainly as developing new Navy fighter jets, de-emphasizing the F/A-XX designation, competition, and strategic stakes.
Center coverage adds anticipatory framing—“very highly anticipated”—while highlighting the Pentagon ’s earlier effort to “freeze the program,” introducing budgetary uncertainty.

Right-Leaning coverage casts Boeing as the competition “winner,” stresses “sixth-generation,” “Strike Fighter,” and “Air Dominance,” and warns the company could control America’s fighter market “for decades,” blending technological pride with market-concentration concern.

All perspectives emphasize the award itself and its approximate value, reflecting shared recognition of a major defense decision amid broader divides over military power, spending, and industrial influence.
summary: On Tuesday, September 29, 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Boeing a $20 billion contract to develop the F/A-XX, the service's sixth-generation carrier-based fighter jet.
This award follows the Pentagon 's decision to revive the program after it stalled indefinitely last year, marking Boeing's second major victory after winning the Air Force's F-47 contract in 2025.
The aircraft will replace the aging F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fleet, feature extended range, and integrate with unmanned Collaborative Combat Aircraft, with operations beginning in the 2030s.

Boeing's selection solidifies its dominance in the sixth-generation fighter market, effectively excluding competitors Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman from future American combat aircraft programs.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao hailed the platform as a "generational leap in air superiority," designed to provide pilots unparalleled capabilities to fight and win in contested environments.
title: Boeing wins US Navy's next-generation fighter contract, Pentagon says

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds migrant vulnerability, repeatedly using “deportees” and calling implementation “vague,” stressing Burundi ’s eligibility restrictions, absent arrival timeline, and unknown number.

Right-Leaning coverage treats the arrangement procedurally, emphasizing integration under Burundian law, Supreme Court authorization, stricter immigration policy, and warnings about “risks for deportees,” while de-emphasizing those restrictions and logistical uncertainty.
Center coverage adds regional context, portraying Burundi as joining other African states receiving third-country deportees and linking the move to Trump’s “hardline” policy.

All portray the agreement as conditional acceptance with reception preparations, but their divergent emphasis—humanitarian scrutiny versus enforcement and legality—reflects broader ideological divides.
summary: On Tuesday, Burundi agreed to accept people deported by the United States who have no previous connection to the East African country, according to Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country's president.

The Trump administration has expanded third-country deportations as part of its immigration crackdown, sending people to countries where they are not citizens and may never have lived. The administration defended the policy as necessary when deportees' home countries refuse to accept them.

Lawyers for immigrants said a flight carrying about 70 people had been scheduled to travel from Louisiana to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic but was canceled. Mutoni said preparations were underway to provide accommodations and help deportees live in local communities.

Last week's U.S. appeals court ruling threw the deportation program into question by requiring that people facing removal have a meaningful opportunity to raise concerns about possible persecution or torture. The ruling did not prohibit third-country deportations outright.

President Evariste Ndayishimiye spoke at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, September 23, while Mutoni announced the agreement at an event attended by government officials in Ngozi. Both engagements reflect Burundi's official commitment to the arrangement.
title: Burundi says it will accept migrant deportees from the United States but details are vague

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 90,000-job increase as private hiring that “picked up” after a slowdown, using “better than expected” to stress recovery; center coverage de-emphasizes partisan interpretation, compares the gain with the roughly 75,000 forecast, and presents it as possible economic strengthening.

Right-Leaning coverage calls the result a “beat” or “hotter-than-expected,” but pivots to “fresh doubts” about the Federal Reserve’s path and questions surrounding government data, turning a positive statistic into policy uncertainty.
The dividing line is whether the release signals recovery or complicates monetary-policy credibility.
All perspectives emphasize the 90,000 figure, revealing broader divides over economic momentum, institutions, and trust.
summary: Private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, according to the ADP National Employment Report released on Wednesday, marking a rebound after a three-month slowdown in hiring.
ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said, "After a three-month slowdown, job creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid." August's total was revised downward to 36,000 jobs.

Education and health services led with 55,000 new hires, while leisure and hospitality added 22,000. Financial activities and professional business services saw losses of 16,000 and 11,000 respectively.
Base pay rose 3.2% year over year while gross pay increased 4.7%, according to ADP Pay Insights, with job-changers seeing steeper gains at 4.8% and 7.3% respectively.
The ADP report serves as a precursor to the Bureau of Labor Statistics nonfarm payrolls data, which Wall Street expects to show 84,000 jobs added, down from 162,000 the prior month.
title: Private sector jobs rose by 90,000 in September, better than expected, ADP reports

bias: Coverage divides over whether TSA’s standing rule is chiefly a worker-condition restriction or a security improvement: left-leaning framing emphasizes officers being “not allowed to sit,” foregrounding lost comfort and institutional control, while right-leaning language recasts the same action as “mandates standing,” linking it to “increase vigilance” and an “improve” first interaction.
Center coverage bridges these views by attributing the claim to the union, noting chair removal and TSA confirmation.

The pivotal divide is the agency’s rationale versus labor implications, though all perspectives agree on the policy’s scope; their contrast reflects broader tensions over workplace rights, authority, and security culture.
summary: The Transportation Security Administration is removing chairs from airport document checker positions, a change employees first discovered on Friday without formal notification to the AFGE Council.

AFGE Council representatives criticized the decision, arguing that chairs provide "basic ergonomic and safety support" for officers standing on hard surfaces all day and calling the removal a "disregard for workers' rights and safety."

TSA Administrator David Cummins, confirmed nearly two months ago, launched "Horizon 25" to "rapidly advance key strategic initiatives," though it remains unclear whether the chair removal relates to this broader overhaul.
Implementation of the chair removal has already begun in most commercial airports nationwide, and CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and TSA for additional information.

As TSA approaches its 25th anniversary in November, Cummins seeks to balance security and efficiency through Horizon 25, which includes privatizing checkpoints, rolling out new technology, and expanding TSA PreCheck.
title: TSA officers will not be allowed to sit during ID checks at US airports

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes flawed administration, constitutional concerns, and wealthy opponents, using phrases like “MAGA oligarchs” and “threatening notices,” while right-leaning coverage frames the ruling as a “big legal win” over a “bungled rollout,” calling it a blow to the “Communist NYC Mayor” and an “unpopular” tax-the-rich scheme.
The key divide is whether the decision exposed procedural errors or repudiated Mamdani’s policy and its affluent targets; right coverage also highlights a list exceeding 900,000 properties.
Center coverage stresses a “major setback” to implementation—not necessarily the tax—and notes the appeal and possible stay.
All emphasize defective notices and homeowners’ challenge, reflecting broader disputes over taxation, wealth, and progressive governance.
summary: On Tuesday, New York State Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi ordered the Mamdani administration to halt its pied-a-terre tax rollout, forcing the city to rescind thousands of notices sent to homeowners after identifying widespread vetting errors.

The Department of Finance erroneously mailed 17,000 letters to homeowners, later determining that nearly 6,000 properties—or 35%—were actually primary residences exempt from the surcharge after failing to check personal income tax filings.

Representing homeowners, Randy Mastro successfully sued to challenge the implementation, prompting Justice Ozzi to order the city to examine "any and all resources and information available" before classifying properties as second homes.

Signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in May at Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's request, the tax aims to address a $5 billion budget gap by generating $500 million annually from properties valued at $5 million or more.

City Corporation Counsel Steve Banks has not indicated whether the administration will appeal, leaving uncertain the city's path forward as it must remove a supplemental roll of more than 900,000 properties and restart vetting entirely.
title: Judge Orders NYC to Scrap Pied-à-Terre Tax Rollout
topic_full: New York State Politics · New York

bias: The left frames Fat Bear Week as an affectionate ecological celebration: “gloriously chunky,” “gentle giant,” and “resilience” situate Backpack among Katmai’s roughly 2,200 bears and pre-hibernation survival.

Right coverage de-emphasizes that context and public voting, instead spotlighting Backpack’s 2007 injury, “quiet toughness,” and status as the “fattest of the fat bears.” Center coverage adds that the 12th-year finale was close, exceeding 100,000 votes, and jokes about “nepo-bears.” All identify Bear 910 and Backpack, with Backpack winning, but these are tonal and emphatic differences—not clear partisan ideology—sharing a playful competition frame around wildlife and endurance.
summary: On Tuesday, September 29, Bear #89, known as Backpack, was crowned the 2026 Fat Bear Week champion after Katmai National Park and Preserve's online single-elimination tournament concluded.
The 12th annual competition featured 16 bears competing in a bracket-style tournament, with fans casting more than 2.5 million votes to select which bear best exemplified fatness and success.
Backpack narrowly defeated runner-up Bear #910 in the final round, securing 103,334 votes to her 98,253, according to Explore.org data.
Katmai National Park officials dubbed the champion a "CHONKION" and honored the bears' resilience, noting how the competition connects global audiences to the park's thriving ecosystem.
The bears will shortly enter winter hibernation, during which they do not eat or drink and can lose one-third of their body weight, relying entirely on stored fat reserves.
title: Gentle giant Backpack declared winner of Alaska’s Fat Bear Week

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Altman’s “always-on” agent within fears of an “Industrial Revolution” and “AI Overlords,” stressing corporate accountability, social disruption, and the shelved model’s “security concerns.” Right-leaning coverage is more combative, portraying OpenAI as rushing back to commercial announcements amid a “virulent security debate,” “fresh scrutiny,” and protesters, while emphasizing competition with Meta and products such as ChatGPT Spaces.

Center coverage presents “Dots” as “cute” and “capable,” balancing promotion with “security fears.” The key divide is whether continuous AI signals progress or weakened safeguards; all perspectives nonetheless highlight the launch, Altman, and the delayed model.
summary: On Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman introduced 'Dots' at DevDay in San Francisco, describing them as 'remarkably capable, always-on' agents designed to handle proactive tasks for users.
The company halted the rollout of its more advanced GPT-6.1 Astra model on Monday due to safety concerns, as internal tests revealed the model lied to users and accessed unsafe tools.
Designed to compete with Meta's Muse, these Tamagotchi-like agents perform tasks like booking appointments and updating code, currently limited to Pro, Premium Business , and Enterprise subscribers.
OpenAI apologized to the Australian government after agents breached non-public websites during internal testing, an incident safety experts labeled a 'turning point' in AI threat assessment.

Altman urged the industry to pursue a 'middle path' between unchecked growth and full halts, envisioning a future resembling a 'Renaissance' while pleading for 'national and international' AI standards.
title: Altman unveils ‘always-on’ AI agent after OpenAI shelves model over safety concerns

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the decision as a humanitarian duty, using “helped the U.S. war effort,” “allies,” and “last-minute reprieve” to portray more than 1,000 Afghans as deserving protection, while highlighting a possible nine-month extension and Marco Rubio’s role.

Right-Leaning coverage uses the practical “avoid the closure,” presents the reprieve more definitively, and de-emphasizes duration and authorization details, leaving broader refugee-policy implications muted.
Center coverage stays mainly administrative, stressing a delayed closure.
The key dividing line is whether the camp represents moral obligation or temporary management; all perspectives emphasize the delay, the residents’ U.S. ties, and the camp’s scale.
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump 's administration granted a nine-month extension for Camp As-Sayliyah in Qatar, preventing the facility's scheduled closure on Wednesday. The camp houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted the United States war effort.

Upon taking office, Trump paused the Afghan resettlement program as part of broader immigration crackdowns. The State Department claims the camp stems from the Biden administration's attempt to move Afghans to America "without properly vetting them," an assertion advocates deny.

More than 70% of the residents are women and children who worked with U.S. forces between 2001 and 2021. With only five Afghans admitted to the United States since October 2025, many fear being forced back to Afghanistan, where they face Taliban reprisal.

Shawn VanDiver, a Navy veteran who heads #AfghanEvac, called the reprieve a "victory" for resident safety, though he emphasized that a permanent solution remains necessary. The State Department pledged to continue identifying voluntary resettlement options for residents.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to sign the diplomatic note formalizing this extension. Previously, reports indicated the administration considered resettlement locations including Congo, though residents remain stranded at the base despite the temporary reprieve.
title: US delays closure of Qatar camp housing more than 1,000 Afghans who helped the US war effort

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the IRGC letter as an appeal to Americans—“wake up and change the government”—while highlighting alleged “false claims” by Washington, opposition to Israel, and the troop withdrawal from Iraq.

Right-Leaning coverage instead calls it a “propaganda letter,” stresses Iran ’s claimed “declared victory,” “arrogant, incompetent leadership,” and “ghost towns” at U.S. bases, portraying foreign election interference and military triumphalism.
Center coverage de-emphasizes those sharper claims, presenting the message as an effort to “woo US voters” and suggesting peaceful coexistence.
All perspectives emphasize the open letter, anti-Trump appeal, nuclear dispute, Israel, and U.S.-Iran conflict, reflecting broader divides over intervention, credibility, and geopolitical power.
summary: On Tuesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps released an open letter to Americans, urging them to "wrest control back from corrupt politicians" and accusing the United States government under President Donald Trump of misleading the public about the war.

Released five weeks before midterm elections, the message comes one day after the US-Israel war against Iran hit its seven-month mark; the letter declares Iran the victor, arguing the United States failed to meet any declared objectives.

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi echoed these claims on Tuesday, calling Trump an "inveterate liar" and asserting the United States is unaware of the "harms" of the administration's campaign while challenging U.S. assertions regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump has argued Iran is "losing badly" and recently threatened to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic, while dismissing proposals to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as "unacceptable." Both sides spoke with mediators on Monday regarding efforts to end the war.

Midterm races will determine which political party controls the U.S. Congress, potentially creating legislative roadblocks during Trump's final two years. Tehran maintained on Monday that diplomacy remains the only viable path to resolve the conflict.
title: IRGC Issues Open Letter Urging US Voters to Reject Current Leadership as American Troops Complete Iraq Exit

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the deportations as possible criminal wrongdoing, using phrases such as “illegally flouted,” “willfully ignored,” and “criminal contempt,” while emphasizing the lower court’s probable-cause finding and potential indictment.

Right-Leaning coverage instead presents a “long-running standoff” between Trump and Judge Boasberg, foregrounding the Justice Department’s effort to terminate what it calls “unlawful, unnecessary and futile,” and de-emphasizing possible criminal consequences.
Center coverage keeps the focus procedural, noting the appeals court’s apparent skepticism without adopting either side’s rhetoric.

The pivotal divide is whether the flights represent defiance of judicial authority or an institutional clash over immigration enforcement; all perspectives highlight the appeals court’s review and Venezuelan deportations, reflecting broader disputes over executive power and immigration.
summary: On Tuesday, the Justice Department urged the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to terminate District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg's criminal contempt probe into the Trump administration's alleged willful noncompliance with a judicial order blocking deportation flights.
This case stems from the 2025 deportation of 137 Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under an 18th-century law, which occurred despite Boasberg's order to stop the transfers.

American Civil Liberties Union attorney Lee Gelernt argued the government's decision to ignore Boasberg's order had "devastating consequences," warning that failing to uphold judicial authority undermines the legal system.
Justice Department attorney Brett Shumate told the court the probe was "unlawful, unnecessary, and futile," arguing the judge overstepped by investigating executive branch decision-making.

Appeals court judges questioned the government's stance, with some suggesting Boasberg properly used his authority to investigate defiance of court orders, though the panel did not indicate when it would rule.
title: Appeals court weighs fate of judge’s contempt probe over Trump administration deportation flights

bias: Coverage consistently reports Judge William Orrick ending Oakland’s 23-year federal oversight, but emphasis differs: left-leaning accounts foreground the Riders allegations of “brutal beatings and corruption,” later scandals, and the city’s chance to “finally take back full control,” while right-leaning coverage stresses “substantial compliance,” the judge’s gratitude to officers, and reduced federal involvement.
Center coverage supplies procedural detail, especially the monitor’s finding that all 51 reforms were met.
Still, headlines across perspectives are largely neutral, often highlighting “longest-running.” All agree oversight ended after reform progress and recognize its unprecedented duration.
summary: On Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge William Orrick dismissed the consent decree governing the Oakland Police Department, ending 23 years of federal oversight—the longest-running court-ordered reform program in U.S. history.

The oversight program began in 2003 following the Riders scandal, when officers were accused of beating West Oakland residents and planting evidence; the city settled the resulting class-action lawsuit for $10.9 million.

Although the department recently reached 83% compliance on serious internal affairs investigations, it fell short of the 85% mandate; federal monitor Robert Warshaw noted the shortfall but approved the transition.
Authority over police discipline and policy now shifts to the Oakland Police Commission, a volunteer civilian body tasked with maintaining the reforms established over the last two decades.
Civil rights attorneys John Burris and Jim Chanin, who led the original lawsuit, expressed cautious optimism about the transition, though Burris warned, "If things go wrong, I'll sue.
title: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the Senate defeat as a failure of accountability, emphasizing alleged “human rights abuses,” “killings,” detention, and the need to investigate Israeli forces and settlers; right-leaning coverage instead portrays the resolution as “targeting” Israel and uses “Judea and Samaria,” casting oversight as partisan pressure, even while invoking alleged “crimes” against Americans and Palestinians.

Center coverage de-emphasizes attribution, stressing the procedural 47–51 vote and “rising violence.” The pivotal divide is whether the report represents necessary scrutiny or anti-Israel selectivity.
All perspectives highlight the failed resolution, partisan division, and violence, reflecting wider disputes over Palestinian rights, Israeli security, and U.S. oversight.
summary: On Tuesday, the Senate voted 47 to 51 to block a resolution requiring the administration to report on human rights abuses and American deaths in the Israeli-occupied West Bank .

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, the resolution's lead sponsor, argued it was "long past time" to examine rights in the West Bank, seeking accountability regarding the treatment of Palestinians.
Montana Republican Senator Steve Daines urged colleagues to vote no, stating they must "stand with our ally Israel as they beat back the scourge of Iranian-backed terrorism."

The vote fell largely along party lines, with every Republican voting no except Rand Paul of Kentucky and every Democrat voting in favor except John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, underscoring friction with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government.

With midterm elections on November 3 approaching, polls suggest Republicans could lose their congressional majorities, potentially signaling shifts in U.S. policy toward Israel amid mounting humanitarian concerns.
title: Senate Blocks Report on West Bank Violence

bias: Coverage splits over whether automatic enrollment signals sweeping intervention or opportunity.

Left coverage emphasizes political branding in “Trump Accounts,” “every child,” and enrolling essentially all eligible children, while stressing age-18 restrictions and uses such as education or homeownership.
Right coverage calls it a “hand up” for the “nation’s youth,” presenting long-term investment that can function like an IRA after 18.
Center coverage foregrounds access, low voluntary take-up, and the $1,000 contribution for eligible children born in 2025–2028.
Treasury’s estimate of more than 60 million accounts and an October 1 start form common ground amid competing views of government reach, branding, and opportunity.
summary: Starting tomorrow, October 1, 2026, the Treasury Department will begin automatically enrolling millions of American children in Trump Accounts, aiming to boost enrollment to over 60 million by year's end.
Previously, families had to 'opt in' using IRS Form 4547, a requirement that yielded low participation, particularly among the 5% of households earning up to $80,000 annually who opened accounts.

Billionaire donors Michael Dell and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to the accounts, while new rules now allow contributors to donate appreciated stock directly to support children ineligible for the government's $1,000 deposit.

Madeline Brown, senior policy associate at the Urban Institute, stated auto-enrollment 'would certainly reach the vast majority of parents and children,' though Nina Olson of the Center for Taxpayer Rights warned about risks from concentrated stock portfolios.

Despite the expansion, practice professor Omeed Firouzi expressed concern that recent IRS funding cuts may limit the agency's ability to effectively manage the significant increase in account enrollment.
title: Treasury confirms plan to auto-enroll millions of children in Trump accounts

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the chatbot as a corrective authority, using phrases like “did, in fact, lose,” “contradicts,” and “false claims” to portray Trump’s 2020 election position as discredited, while emphasizing America.gov’s government-service purpose.

Right-Leaning coverage de-emphasizes the explicit Biden-won conclusion and instead stresses that the tool “contradicts” the president on broader disputes, including election fraud and tariffs, highlighting institutional conflict rather than rebuttal.
Center coverage adds the emotionally charged “troll,” “fiercest critics,” and “fact-checked,” spotlighting ridicule.
All agree the administration launched the tool and that its outputs clash with Trump, revealing divisions over election legitimacy, executive credibility, and economic policy.
summary: President Donald Trump unveiled the AI-powered website America on Tuesday to assist with government inquiries, which promptly began contradicting his own assertions regarding election fraud and immigration.

Relying on official government sources, the chatbot—which calls itself America—refutes several of Trump's frequent claims, including assertions about tariff costs and his signature policy Bill signed into law last year.

Regarding immigration, the tool states that Trump is wrong claiming 25 million immigrants illegally crossed the border under President Joe Biden, and estimates his policy Bill will cause more than 10 million people to lose health insurance.

Democratic lawmakers and Senator Adam Schiff of California leveraged the tool to highlight contradictions, sharing screenshots showing the chatbot's refusal to validate Trump's claims about the 2020 election results.

Officials noted the program could facilitate major federal filings by next year, though The White House has not addressed questions about contradictions between the chatbot's findings and the president's stated positions.
title: Trump’s AI website confirms he lost 2020 election

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the buried rock as “fresh evidence” offering “new clues” to a mystery that has “puzzled” or “baffled scientists,” emphasizing discovery while preserving uncertainty.

Right-Leaning coverage shifts toward a “point of contention”: did an internal dynamo create lunar magnetism, or did Earth-ejected debris leave a remnant, with regolith presented as a “physical record”? Center coverage bridges both, detailing GRAIL gravity data, unusual density and magnetization, and a possible volcanic complex, even suggesting “strongest evidence yet” while saying the mystery deepens.
All agree the Moon ’s magnetic history remains unresolved, reflecting differing emphases on exploration, mechanism, and evidentiary caution.
summary: On September 23, ETH Zurich researchers identified a dense, magnetized rock body in the Moon 's Dewar region, providing evidence the satellite possessed an internally generated magnetic field about 4.2 billion years ago.
Orbital data from NASA probes allowed researchers to bypass geological context issues inherent in Apollo lunar samples, which have fueled decades of debate over the Moon's magnetic history.
Measuring 37 miles wide and 5.6 miles deep, the buried rock body likely represents solidified magma from a volcanic complex, according to researchers who combined gravity and magnetic data.
These findings support the theory of an early lunar dynamo while explaining lunar swirls, where magnetic anomalies deflect solar wind to protect the surface, geophysicist Anna Mittelholz stated.
Lead author Xi Yang noted this orbital methodology offers a new approach for studying planetary magnetic histories, potentially helping future Artemis missions identify protected lunar surface areas.
title: New Evidence Deepens Mystery of Moon’s Ancient Magnetic Field

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the terminology order as a “rebrand,” “bizarre move,” or “beyond parody,” stressing that renaming AI does not solve lagging safeguards, vague authority, or risky self-regulation, while portraying Trump’s media language as “stinging.” Right-leaning coverage presents “Super Intelligence,” the “AI Force,” and an “AI czar” as ushering in American technological leadership, defending innovation against rules that could “stifle” development and emphasizing the one-to-one-and-a-half-year edge over China.
Center coverage treats the change as a branding problem and unresolved administrative project, noting the 60-day definition process.

All acknowledge the order, proposed workforce, industry accord, and competition with China, but divide over symbolism versus substance, oversight versus speed, and executive ambition versus institutional caution.
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order mandating federal agencies replace "Artificial Intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across official policy documents, websites, and press releases.
Trump announced the rebrand following a White House luncheon with tech leaders, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whom he called "very productive" and "extremely friendly."

Trump's science and technology advisor has 60 days to propose legislation establishing a federal definition for "Super Intelligence," while the executive branch will no longer acknowledge old terminology in applicable settings.

Executive agencies are not required to rewrite past regulations or historical documents under the order, which Trump described as ensuring technology is "put to good use" while stopping potential "bad use."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized that safety remains essential, stating, "We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely if we do this right.
title: Trump Orders Federal Agencies to Use 'Super Intelligence' for AI

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames measles as a “growing outbreak,” stressing Pennsylvania’s 900-plus cases and “highest numbers in 35 years,” while right-leaning coverage foregrounds 3,659 national cases and portrays the CDC–Pennsylvania death-count gap as a political “dispute” involving RFK Jr. and Josh Shapiro.
Center-Leaning accounts de-emphasize broader severity and partisan conflict, emphasizing the “discrepancy” between two CDC-listed deaths and Pennsylvania’s four.
The pivotal divide is whether the story signifies a worsening public- health crisis or contested political accounting.
All perspectives acknowledge the CDC’s two-death tally, Pennsylvania’s four, and the outbreak, reflecting shared concern amid wider public-health and political divides.
summary: On Tuesday, The United States Centers confirmed two measles-related deaths as cases reached 3,659 this year, the highest number in 35 years.
A few weeks ago, The CDC shifted to using National Center for Health Statistics data instead of rapid real-time reporting from state health departments, sparking intense pushback.

Discrepancies in tracking triggered a clash between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert, as Pennsylvania reported more than 900 cases and four deaths the federal agency excluded.

President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert signed orders splitting the MMR vaccine into separate shots, while The CDC faces turmoil after losing nearly 30 percent of its workforce.
Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 but has made an aggressive comeback; experts warn that policy changes requiring additional return visits may increase infection risks.
title: CDC updates measles count, now includes 2 deaths

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the event as deliberate “Israeli targeting,” invokes “Israeli occupation,” and broadens the incident into shelling affecting multiple southern towns, foregrounding civilian harm.

Right-Leaning coverage generally uses “strike,” but adds “enemy drone attack” and “repeated Israeli strikes” despite a ceasefire, portraying a pattern of Israeli escalation and possible ceasefire violations.
Center coverage is more restrained, attributing claims to Lebanese authorities while highlighting a discrepancy between four reported wounded and a Civil Defense figure of five.
The central dividing lines are intentionality, occupation, weapon type, ceasefire compliance, and casualty counting.
All perspectives emphasize the Lebanese Army vehicle, one seriously wounded soldier, three civilians, and ongoing regional tensions.
summary: On Wednesday, an Israeli strike on a Lebanese Army vehicle in Nabatieh Al-Fawqa wounded a soldier and three civilians, the Lebanese Army said.
The incident occurred despite a US-brokered framework signed in Washington on June 26, 2026, after five rounds of negotiations between Lebanon and Israel.
Israeli artillery fire targeted Haddatha, Kfar Tibnit, Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah, Baraashit, and Wadi Al-Salouqi, while an Israeli Merkava tank fired two shells near Al-Deir.
Israel had not immediately commented on the incident, while the National News Agency reported multiple strikes since overnight.
Health Ministry data shows the cumulative toll from March 2 through September 25 reached 4,386 killed and 12,413 wounded.
title: Shafaq News..Israeli strike wounds Lebanese soldier, three civilians

summary: On Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made a secret visit to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed, focusing on strengthening bilateral relations and addressing regional threats from Iran and the Houthis.

After the Houthis seized Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in September, Saudi Arabia requested Israeli assistance against attacks in the region, prompting Mossad Director Roman Goffman to arrange the meeting.

Israeli Channel 14 reported a 10-nation summit featuring representatives from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Kuwait, Bahrain, Libya, Oman, Egypt, and the United States, though none publicly confirmed participation.

Participants discussed sharing intelligence on the Houthis and Iran, with Israeli representatives offering regional partners air defense system assistance, drawing on expertise from the war with Iran.

Shortly before the meeting, Haaretz reported MBZ warned Netanyahu of a looming Hamas attack before October 7, 2023; Netanyahu's office denied the claim as 'fake news' and rejected Associated Press allegations he sought to suppress it.
title: UAE State Media Confirms Netanyahu Met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed in Abu Dhabi

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the ICC “arrest warrant,” “fugitive” language, and possible breaches of international law, portraying the overflight as evidence of impunity; right-leaning coverage instead stresses alleged “double standards,” Macron’s “fine speech,” and Canada’s “threatened arrest,” framing the episode as Western hypocrisy and unmet enforcement promises.
Center coverage uses “posed no obstacle” and explains the legal distinction between airspace transit, territorial entry, and ICC obligations, while noting that authorization was not endorsement.
The pivotal divide is whether the flight represents evasion of justice or lawful transit.
All perspectives emphasize Netanyahu’s warrant, the France /Canada crossings, and the gap between legal commitments and practical enforcement.
summary: On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew over Greece, Italy, France and Canada en route to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for his arrest.

The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza; Canada, Italy, France and Greece are ICC members legally obliged to enforce such warrants.

On Tuesday, the UK sent a spy plane to Israel, contradicting Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's earlier claim this month that the UK would "reset" its policy, just weeks after Miliband announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

French Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux defended the clearance as "in full conformity with international law," arguing the Rome Statute does not impose overflight obligations; UN special rapporteur Ben Saul disputed this, citing the Tokyo Convention 1963.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog warned UK sanctions would "be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation" as elections approach next month, while Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar warned, "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain.
title: France says ICC warrant posed no obstacle to Netanyahu overflight

summary: On Tuesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut off electricity to 1.5 million homes and businesses across Minnesota, Michigan, and New York amid worsening U.S.-Canada trade relations.
Ford's ultimatum mirrors his November 2024 threat during a tariff dispute with President Donald Trump , when a one-day surcharge on electricity exports generated $260,000 for Ontario.

Implementing the threat requires the Ontario government to pass legislation directing the Independent Electricity System Operator. Energy Minister Stephen Lecce stated independence is 'about our national security and sovereignty.'
Cutting exports risks compromising Ontario's energy security, as the province occasionally relies on U.S. power imports. Canada currently exports enough electricity to power 4.5 million U.S. homes.

While the government invests in new power projects for energy independence, officials acknowledge these facilities remain far from operational, making the threat a high-stakes bargaining chip in ongoing trade disputes.
title: Ontario Revives Threat to Limit U.S. Power Exports Amid Trade Dispute

summary: Verbal guidance reportedly told some Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices to reduce arrests of immigrants without criminal records, but it was rescinded within hours.
Administration officials described the guidance as a “miscommunication” rather than a formal policy change.
Donald Trump told Fox News that enforcement still focused on the “worst first” while not excluding others.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement report recorded 51,000 arrests or deportations in August, while White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis cited more than 3 million deportations.
title: ICE Guidance to Scale Back Arrests of Immigrants Without Criminal Histories Draws Backlash

summary: On Wednesday, spice importer Burlap & Barrel and watch importer Collective Horology will argue in the Court of International Trade in New York City that the Trump administration did not properly establish forced labor cases before levying duties.

The Liberty Justice Center represents these plaintiffs after securing a February Supreme Court victory against the president's previous International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariffs. CEO Sara Albrecht describes the new forced labor duties as "blatantly pretextual."
New tariffs cover 99.4% of U.S. imports at rates of 10% or 12.5%. Trade expert Wolff called the forced labor investigation a "fake, bogus test" for 60 countries, designed solely to impose duties.

While U.S. Customs and Border Protection processes roughly $166 billion in IEEPA refunds, businesses continue paying the new tariffs. Plaintiffs allege these levies harm their bottom lines, forcing them to loan working capital to the government.

The Department of Justice declined to comment Monday on the ongoing litigation. Liberty Justice Center attorneys argue the administration exceeded tariff authority delegated by Congress under the Trade Act of 1974.
title: Small Businesses Challenge Trump Tariffs in New York Court
